title: Making Plans with Friends

dialogue.title: Planning a Saturday Outing
dialogue.context: Ahmed, Lisa, and Carlos plan to visit Portland Saturday Market together.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Are you guys free this Saturday? How about we go to the Saturday Market downtown?

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: I'd love to! What time are you thinking?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.text: Saturday Market sounds fun, but I have soccer until noon. Could we meet in the afternoon?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Sure! How about 12:30? That gives you time after soccer.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: Perfect! Should we meet there, or do you want to carpool?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.text: I can drive if someone helps with gas money.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Of course! I'll give you $10. Where should we meet?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.text: Let's meet at the Target parking lot on 82nd. It's easy for everyone.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: Sounds good to me! After the market, would you like to get lunch?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Great idea! There are food carts near the market. We can decide when we're there.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.text: Perfect plan! See you Saturday at 12:30 at Target. I'll text you when I'm leaving.

listening_exercises.transcript: When making plans with friends, be specific about time and place. Instead of saying 'Let's hang out sometime,' say 'Would you like to meet Saturday at 3 PM at Starbucks on Main Street?' Specific plans are more likely to happen. Also, confirm plans the day before to make sure everyone remembers.
listening_exercises.question: Why should you be specific when making plans?
options: Plans are more likely to happen

listening_exercises.transcript: If you need to decline an invitation, be honest but kind. Say 'I'd love to, but I already have plans' rather than making up elaborate excuses. If you want to maintain the friendship, suggest an alternative: 'I can't make it Saturday, but how about next weekend?' This shows you genuinely want to spend time together.
listening_exercises.question: What should you do when declining an invitation?
options: Be honest and suggest an alternative

listening_exercises.transcript: Common phrases for making plans: 'Are you free this weekend?' asks about availability. 'Would you like to join us?' is a polite invitation. 'Let's' suggests doing something together. 'How about...?' offers a suggestion. 'Sounds good!' accepts the plan. 'I'll see you there' confirms attendance.
listening_exercises.question: What does 'Are you free?' mean?

speaking_tasks.prompt: Invite a friend to do something this weekend. Suggest an activity, time, and place. Record yourself for 25 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: Hey Maria, are you free this Saturday? I was thinking we could go to that new coffee shop on Division Street. How about meeting at 2 PM? They have great pastries and we can catch up. It would be nice to spend some time together. Let me know if that works for you, or if another time is better!

speaking_tasks.prompt: Your friend invites you to dinner, but you can't go. Decline politely and suggest meeting another time. Record for 20 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: Thanks so much for the invitation! I'd really love to join you, but unfortunately I have a family obligation that evening. I'm so sorry to miss it. How about we plan something for next week instead? Maybe we could get lunch on Saturday? I really do want to get together soon.

writing_tasks.prompt: Write a text message inviting a friend to an event. Include: what the activity is, when and where, and why they should come. (50-70 words)
writing_tasks.example: Hey Carlos! There's a food festival at Pioneer Square this Saturday from 11-4. They'll have food trucks from all over the world - I know you love trying new food! Lisa and I are planning to go around noon. Would you like to join us? The weather is supposed to be beautiful. Let me know if you're interested! It should be a lot of fun and we can walk around downtown after.

writing_tasks.prompt: Your friend invited you to a party, but you have to work. Write a message declining the invitation and suggesting meeting another time. (40-60 words)
writing_tasks.example: Hi Jennifer, thank you so much for inviting me to your birthday party! I'm really sorry but I have to work that night - my manager already scheduled me and I can't switch shifts. I feel terrible about missing it. Can we celebrate together next weekend? Maybe lunch or dinner? I'd love to take you out to make up for missing the party. Happy early birthday!

grammar_focus.title: 'Would you like to...?' for Invitations
grammar_focus.explanation: Use 'Would you like to...?' for polite invitations. It's more formal than 'Do you want to...?'
examples: Would you like to go to the movies? (polite invitation)
Would you like to join us for dinner? (inviting to join)
Would you like to come over? (inviting to home)
Do you want to hang out? (more casual)

grammar_focus.title: 'Let's...' for Suggestions
grammar_focus.explanation: 'Let's' (Let us) suggests doing something together. It's friendly and casual.
examples: Let's go to the park. (suggesting together)
Let's meet at 3 PM. (suggesting meeting time)
Let's try that restaurant. (suggesting activity)
Let's not stay too late. (negative suggestion)

grammar_focus.title: 'How about + gerund' for Suggestions
grammar_focus.explanation: Use 'How about' + verb-ing to suggest activities. It asks for agreement.
examples: How about meeting at 2 PM? (suggesting time)
How about trying that new café? (suggesting place)
How about going to the beach? (suggesting activity)
How about we take the bus? (suggesting method)

cultural_notes: In American culture, it's common to make plans in advance, sometimes weeks ahead.
It's okay to decline invitations. Just be polite and honest about why.
Confirming plans the day before is considerate - it reminds everyone.
Being on time is important. If you're running late, text or call.
Splitting costs (like gas money) is normal among friends.
Saying 'Let's hang out sometime' without specific plans usually means just being friendly, not a real invitation.
